stem: After a stakeholder workshop for a contract Q&A assistant, a developer must decide which statement will drive the deployment architecture (capacity, rate limits, streaming) rather than the prompt and feature logic. Which statement is it?

options.text: Answers must be written in the same language the customer used to ask the question, including dialects.
options.why: This describes what the assistant does with each answer, a functional behavior handled in prompt and feature logic.

options.text: It must support 300 concurrent sessions at peak with p95 time to first token under 2 seconds.
options.why: Concurrency and latency targets are non-functional infrastructure requirements that size rate limits, capacity, and the streaming design.

options.text: The assistant must decline to give legal advice and point users to the legal team instead.
options.why: A refusal rule is functional behavior implemented through instructions and guardrails, not deployment capacity.

options.text: Every answer must quote the exact contract clause it relies on so reviewers can verify it quickly.
options.why: Citation is an output requirement verified with evals; it does not change the deployment architecture.

explanation: Separating functional requirements (what the system does) from infrastructure or non-functional requirements (how much, how fast, where) tells the developer which statements size the deployment. Concurrency and latency percentiles drive rate-limit planning, capacity, and streaming; language, refusals, and citations drive prompts, guardrails, and evals.
reference: Exam guide — Understanding Requirements; Claude API docs — Rate limits

stem: A retailer requires that all AI usage be billed through its existing Google Cloud commitment and governed by Google Cloud IAM, and that inference stay inside the European Union. Which deployment best fits these requirements?

options.text: Use Claude on Google Cloud Vertex AI through an EU regional or multi-region endpoint.
options.why: Vertex AI satisfies the Google Cloud billing and IAM requirement, and EU regional or multi-region endpoints keep routing inside the EU.

options.text: Call the Claude API directly and state in the system prompt that data must stay in the EU.
options.why: Direct API usage is billed by Anthropic, not through Google Cloud, and a prompt cannot control where inference runs.

options.text: Use Claude on Google Cloud Vertex AI through the global endpoint for the best availability.
options.why: The global endpoint routes dynamically across geographies, so it does not keep inference inside the EU.

options.text: Give each employee a claude.ai seat and ask them to paste customer data into chats.
options.why: claude.ai seats are not billed through Google Cloud, and a chat product does not integrate with the retailer's systems.

explanation: Procurement, identity, and residency constraints often decide the platform before any code is written. Claude on Vertex AI is billed and governed through Google Cloud, and its regional and multi-region endpoints keep traffic within a geography, whereas the global endpoint trades residency for availability.
reference: Claude docs — Claude on Vertex AI (global, multi-region, and regional endpoints)

stem: A legal operations lead says a new contract-extraction feature "must be 100% accurate." Contracts vary widely, and a missed renewal date on a high-value contract is very costly. How should the developer turn this into a requirement the team can build and test against?

options.text: Accept the 100% target as written and choose the most capable model tier so it can be met.
options.why: No model guarantees perfect extraction on varied documents, so the requirement would be untestable and would always fail.

options.text: Set temperature to 0 and document that the output is deterministic and therefore accurate.
options.why: Deterministic sampling does not make output correct; the same mistake is simply repeated consistently.

options.text: Set per-field accuracy targets measured by evals, and send high-value or uncertain contracts to human review.
options.why: Measurable targets make the requirement testable, and targeted review manages the costly errors that automation cannot eliminate.

options.text: Reject the requirement and ship without any target, since LLM output is inherently unpredictable anyway.
options.why: Dropping the target leaves no acceptance criteria and ignores the business risk the lead is raising.

explanation: Absolute business statements need to become measurable, testable requirements. Negotiate accuracy targets per field that evals can verify, and address the costly residual errors with process design, such as human review for high-value or uncertain cases, rather than promising perfection.
reference: Claude docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: An agent proposes about 8,000 customer refunds a day. Policy says any refund over $500, or on an account flagged for fraud, needs a human approver; all others should be paid within minutes. The review team can handle about 400 approvals a day. Which design meets the requirements?

options.text: Route every proposed refund to the review team so a human sees each decision before any money moves.
options.why: Sending 8,000 items a day to a team that can handle 400 creates an ever-growing backlog and breaks the within-minutes requirement.

options.text: Route over-$500 and flagged refunds to reviewers by rules in code, auto-pay the rest, and audit a sample.
options.why: Deterministic routing enforces the policy exactly, keeps the human queue within capacity, and sampling catches systematic errors in auto-paid refunds.

options.text: Tell Claude in the system prompt to decide which refunds look risky enough to need a human reviewer.
options.why: The policy defines exact criteria; leaving routing to model judgment means a mandatory review can be skipped.

options.text: Auto-pay every refund immediately and have the review team check all of the previous week's refunds in bulk.
options.why: After-the-fact review violates the rule that high-value and flagged refunds need approval before payment.

explanation: Human-in-the-loop requirements must be placed where policy demands them and sized to reviewer capacity. Enforce the policy thresholds deterministically in code, send only the in-scope cases to humans, let the remainder proceed, and sample auto-approved cases for quality assurance.
reference: Exam guide — Understanding Requirements; Claude docs — Building trustworthy applications

stem: A customer-facing assistant and a nightly 400,000-record backfill share one organization's Messages API limits, and the assistant gets 429 errors whenever the backfill runs. The assistant must keep its capacity, and the backfill must finish within 24 hours. Which changes meet both requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Move the backfill to the Message Batches API, which has its own rate limits and a 24-hour window.
options.why: Batches draw on a separate set of rate limits and fit a latency-tolerant 24-hour job, so the backfill stops consuming the assistant's Messages API capacity.

options.text: Raise max_retries in the assistant so its requests keep retrying until the backfill has finished for the night.
options.why: More retries only delay users and add load; the assistant still competes with the backfill for the same limits.

options.text: Run each workload in its own workspace and set a lower rate limit on the backfill workspace.
options.why: Workspace limits cap one workspace's share of the organization's limits, protecting capacity for the assistant's workspace.

options.text: Increase the backfill's concurrency so it finishes sooner and frees the organization limits earlier.
options.why: Higher concurrency makes the contention more intense while it lasts, producing more 429s for the assistant.

options.text: Switch the assistant to a smaller model tier so each of its requests uses fewer tokens per minute.
options.why: Changing the assistant's model trades away quality without removing the backfill's competing load.

explanation: Throughput requirements for several workloads call for isolation. The Message Batches API has its own rate limits and suits latency-tolerant work finishing within 24 hours, and per-workspace rate limits keep one workload from starving another, while organization-wide limits still apply overall. Retrying harder or pushing more concurrency makes contention worse.
reference: Claude API docs — Rate limits (Message Batches API; setting lower limits for workspaces)

stem: A SaaS company wants an in-product agent, driven from its TypeScript backend, that edits files in each customer's sandboxed workspace, runs validation commands, and waits for approval of each action in the company's own web UI. The team does not want to build file and shell tools from scratch. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Call the Messages API directly and hand-build the agent loop, the file and shell tools, and the approval flow.
options.why: This can work, but it contradicts the stated requirement to use built-in file and shell tools instead of writing them.

options.text: Have each customer install the Claude Code CLI and run it in a terminal against their own workspace.
options.why: Customers would leave the product for a terminal, and approvals would happen in the CLI rather than in the company's web UI.

options.text: Use the Claude Agent SDK for TypeScript, with its built-in tools and an approval callback tied to the UI.
options.why: The Agent SDK provides Claude Code's agent loop and built-in tools as a library with programmatic tool-approval callbacks, matching every constraint.

options.text: Submit each configuration fix as a Message Batches request and show the result once processing ends.
options.why: Batches are asynchronous single requests without an interactive tool loop, so there is no per-action approval or command execution.

explanation: Choosing the surface is a requirements decision. When a product needs an embedded agent with built-in file and command tools, programmatic control from its own backend, and custom approval UX, the Claude Agent SDK fits better than the raw Messages API (build everything yourself), the Claude Code CLI (a developer tool), or batches (no interactive loop).
reference: Claude Code docs — Run Claude Code programmatically (Agent SDK)

stem: Two weeks after building a meeting-notes summarizer, a team cannot agree whether a revised prompt is an improvement: one engineer likes its tone, another says it misses action items. Which life-cycle artifact, produced during design, would have settled this?

options.text: Measurable success criteria plus an eval set of representative meetings to score against.
options.why: Agreed, measurable criteria and a test set turn "better" into a score both prompts can be compared on.

options.text: A detailed architecture diagram of how the summarizer connects to the calendar system.
options.why: Integration architecture matters, but it says nothing about whether a summary is good enough.

options.text: A runbook describing how to roll back the summarizer if the service goes down.
options.why: Rollback runbooks support operations; they do not define what counts as a quality improvement.

options.text: A style guide that fixes the tone and vocabulary the summaries should use.
options.why: Tone is only one dimension; a style guide would not measure missed action items or overall quality.

explanation: In an LLM system life cycle, success criteria and an evaluation set are design-phase outputs. Without them, every later change turns into a debate of opinions; with them, test, rollout, and maintenance decisions can be made on measured results.
reference: Claude docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: Before migrating a claims-triage service to a newer model, a team wants evidence of how the new model behaves on real, current production inputs, but it must not expose any user to the new model until that evidence is reviewed. What should they do?

options.text: Route 50% of users to the new model for a week and compare the results between the two groups.
options.why: An A/B split exposes half the users to the unreviewed model, which the constraint forbids.

options.text: Rely only on the eval set assembled at launch, since it was already approved by the team.
options.why: A launch-time eval set may not reflect current production inputs, which is the evidence they asked for.

options.text: Switch fully to the new model overnight and roll back quickly if monitoring shows a problem.
options.why: A full switch exposes every user before any review, the opposite of the requirement.

options.text: Shadow-test by also sending live requests to the new model, logging but not serving its outputs.
options.why: Shadow traffic gives real, current inputs for both models while users continue to receive only the current model's answers.

explanation: Shadow (dark) testing runs the candidate on mirrored production traffic without serving its output, giving realistic evidence with zero user exposure, at the cost of extra spend during the test. A/B tests and canaries come later, once exposing some users is acceptable.
reference: Claude API docs — Model deprecations (migrating to replacements)

stem: A model used by an invoice-extraction service retires in six weeks. On the eval set, the recommended replacement matches field accuracy, but about 5% of its outputs break the downstream parser because formatting differs from what the prompt was tuned to produce. What is the best plan?

options.text: Keep using the current model past the retirement date while the formatting issue is investigated in depth.
options.why: Requests to a retired model fail, so staying past retirement causes an outage.

options.text: Switch now and accept the 5% parser failures, since field accuracy is equal on the eval set.
options.why: Parser breaks are production failures; equal accuracy on paper does not help invoices that cannot be processed.

options.text: Enforce the format with a schema, re-run evals with parser tests, and stage the rollout before retirement.
options.why: This fixes the cause (the output contract), proves it with parser-inclusive evals, and still finishes the migration in time.

options.text: Relax the downstream parser to accept any shape of output so the formatting differences stop causing errors.
options.why: An anything-goes parser hides malformed data and moves the failure into the systems that consume the invoices.

explanation: Model migration is maintenance with a hard deadline. Treat the output format as a contract (for example with structured outputs), add downstream-compatibility checks to the evals, and complete a staged rollout before the retirement date, when requests to the old model start failing.
reference: Claude API docs — Model deprecations; Structured outputs

stem: A canary sends 10% of traffic to a new model version. After two days, quality scores and error rates match the control, but p95 latency is up 60% and cost per request is up 45%. Logged usage shows output_tokens per request roughly doubled. The requirements include latency and cost budgets. What is the best next step?

options.text: Roll forward to 100%, because quality and error rates are unchanged and those are the primary metrics.
options.why: Latency and cost budgets are requirements too; widening the rollout multiplies a known budget breach.

options.text: Hold at 10%, find why outputs got longer, tune the prompt or max_tokens, and re-evaluate.
options.why: The trace points to verbosity; pausing limits exposure while the cause is fixed and verified against all requirements.

options.text: Roll back and permanently rule out the new model version, since it clearly failed the canary.
options.why: The regression has a specific, likely fixable cause; discarding the upgrade outright gives up its benefits without diagnosis.

options.text: Request a higher rate limit so the longer responses stop affecting latency.
options.why: Rate limits govern how much traffic is allowed; they do not make individual long generations faster or cheaper.

explanation: Canary metrics must be judged against all requirements, not just quality. Here the usage data shows the cause: roughly twice the output tokens, which drives both latency and cost. Pause the rollout, address output length, re-run evals, and only then widen exposure.
reference: Claude API docs — Reducing latency; Messages API (usage)

stem: An on-call engineer sees a spike of 529 overloaded_error responses from the Claude API. The 429 rate is flat, and the last deploy was two days ago with no issues since. Which conclusions or actions are appropriate? (Choose two.)

options.text: Roll back the deploy from two days ago, since the new errors must have been introduced by it.
options.why: A 529 signals temporary API-side overload, and the deploy had been healthy for two days, so a rollback targets the wrong cause.

options.text: Treat it as temporary API-wide overload, not the organization's rate limit or a service defect.
options.why: overloaded_error (529) occurs under high traffic across all users, unlike 429, which reflects the organization's own limits.

options.text: Ask Anthropic for a higher rate limit so the organization stops receiving the 529 responses.
options.why: Rate limits govern 429 responses; a higher limit does not prevent API-wide overload.

options.text: Keep backoff retries and queue latency-tolerant work until the error rate recovers.
options.why: Backoff handles transient overload, and deferring non-urgent work reduces load and user impact while it lasts.

options.text: Treat the responses as malformed requests and start inspecting request payloads for invalid fields.
options.why: Malformed requests return 400 invalid_request_error; 529 has nothing to do with the payload.

explanation: Operating a Claude system means reading error codes correctly. 529 overloaded_error is transient and shared across API users, 429 reflects your own rate limits, and 400 is a bad request. For 529, rely on backoff and graceful degradation rather than rolling back healthy releases or requesting new limits.
reference: Claude API docs — Errors

stem: A support assistant's eval suite has scored a steady 97% for six months, yet escalations to human agents have doubled. Sampled transcripts show many questions about a product line launched last quarter, which the eval set does not contain. Which maintenance actions are most appropriate? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add labeled cases sampled from recent production traffic, including the new product line.
options.why: The eval set has drifted from real usage; refreshing it from production makes the score reflect what users now ask.

options.text: Trust the 97% score and treat the escalation increase as a staffing problem outside the system.
options.why: The transcripts show the assistant failing on unseen topics, so the stable score is measuring the wrong things.

options.text: Add more variations of the existing test cases to make the current eval set larger.
options.why: More of the same cases still excludes the new product line, so it cannot detect the actual failures.

options.text: Schedule recurring eval-set reviews against sampled production traffic as part of ongoing maintenance.
options.why: Input drift is continuous; a regular refresh keeps the eval suite a trustworthy release gate.

options.text: Move to the most capable model tier immediately, since the current model cannot handle new topics.
options.why: The cause is undiagnosed and may be missing knowledge or retrieval content; a bigger model is a costly guess.

explanation: An eval suite is only as good as its match to production. When real inputs drift, such as a new product line, a stable score can hide rising failures. Maintenance includes refreshing eval data from sampled production traffic and doing so on a regular schedule.
reference: Claude docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: After Claude writes a profile summary, a worker calls PUT /profiles/42/summary (replacing the whole summary) and POST /events (appending an audit event). A timeout hides whether either call succeeded. Which call can be retried as-is without risking a duplicate effect?

options.text: Both calls, because a timeout means the server never received either request.
options.why: A timeout says nothing about whether the server processed the request; a retried POST can append a second event.

options.text: Only the POST, because appending an event is the safer of the two operations.
options.why: POST is not idempotent; repeating it can create a duplicate audit event.

options.text: Neither call; after a timeout the worker should discard the job and continue.
options.why: Dropping the job loses both the summary and the audit event when a safe retry path exists.

options.text: Only the PUT, because repeating a full replacement leaves the same state.
options.why: PUT is idempotent: repeating the full replacement leaves the same final state.

explanation: HTTP method semantics determine retry safety. PUT (full replacement), GET, and DELETE are idempotent, so repeating them yields the same state; POST is not, so it needs an idempotency key or deduplication before automatic retries.
reference: Exam guide — Software Engineering Foundations (REST APIs)

stem: A service consumes streamed Messages API responses. It checks that the HTTP status is 200, then concatenates text deltas until the connection closes and saves the result. During busy periods some saved answers are cut off mid-sentence. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.text: An error event such as overloaded_error can arrive mid-stream; handle it, discard the partial text, and retry.
options.why: Errors can arrive inside an already-open stream, so a 200 status does not mean the response completed.

options.text: max_tokens is too low for busy periods; raise it so the model can finish longer answers under load.
options.why: Load does not change max_tokens; a max_tokens cutoff would appear as that stop reason on any day, not only busy ones.

options.text: The HTTP client times out while reading; switch to non-streaming requests so every response arrives in one piece.
options.why: Dropping streaming removes incremental output and does not handle API errors, which still occur in non-streaming mode.

options.text: Text deltas arrive out of order under load; sort them by timestamp before concatenating.
options.why: Stream events arrive in order; ordering is not what causes truncated answers.

explanation: With streaming, the HTTP status is sent before generation finishes, so errors such as overloaded_error can arrive as an error event mid-stream. Robust async stream handling checks for error events and a proper message_stop, never persists partial output as complete, and retries with backoff; the SDKs raise these errors for you.
reference: Claude API docs — Streaming messages (error events)

stem: A developer runs two Claude Code sessions in the same checkout, one building a feature and one fixing an unrelated bug. Edits from one session keep appearing in the other's diffs and occasionally overwrite each other. What is the recommended setup?

options.text: Keep one checkout, but have each session stash its changes before the other one makes edits.
options.why: Manual stashing between concurrent sessions is error-prone and still lets both sessions write to the same files.

options.text: Run each session in its own git worktree, each on a separate branch of the same repository.
options.why: Worktrees give each session a separate working directory and branch, so edits cannot collide while history stays shared.

options.text: Commit both sessions' work to the same branch more often so the conflicts stay small.
options.why: Frequent commits do not stop two sessions from editing the same working files at the same moment.

options.text: Clone the repository a second time and copy the finished bug-fix files back into the first clone.
options.why: Copying files between clones bypasses version control and risks losing or mixing changes.

explanation: Parallel Claude Code sessions should be isolated in separate git worktrees (for example with the --worktree flag), each on its own branch. Changes then merge through normal branches and pull requests instead of colliding in one working directory.
reference: Claude Code docs — Worktrees

stem: A Python job must summarize 2,000 documents with AsyncAnthropic. Requirements: stay within rate limits, a single bad document must not abort the run, permanently failing documents must be recorded for follow-up, and a rerun must skip documents already done. Which design meets all of these?

options.text: await asyncio.gather() over all 2,000 coroutines with default arguments and rerun the whole job if it raises.
options.why: Unbounded concurrency breaks rate limits, and the first exception propagates to the caller, so completed results are lost and nothing is recorded.

options.text: Wrap the whole run in one try/except and restart all 2,000 documents from the beginning on any error.
options.why: One failure still aborts the run, and restarting from scratch reprocesses completed documents instead of skipping them.

options.text: Use a semaphore-bounded pool with per-document try/except, log permanent failures by ID, and skip done IDs.
options.why: Bounded concurrency respects limits, per-item handling isolates failures (SDK retries cover transient ones), and recorded IDs make the job resumable.

options.text: Process documents one at a time in a loop and stop at the first error so it can be fixed before continuing.
options.why: Stopping on the first error violates the requirement that one bad document must not abort the run, and serial processing is slow.

explanation: Production async code needs bounded concurrency, per-item error isolation, and idempotent resumption. An unbounded asyncio.gather propagates the first exception and floods the rate limits, and a run-level try/except restarts everything, so neither meets these requirements. A bounded worker pool that records outcomes per document does.
reference: Claude API docs — Client SDKs (Python); Rate limits

stem: Claude Code opens a pull request fixing a date-parsing bug, and CI is green. During review, the engineer notices the PR also changed three existing test assertions so they match the new output. Which responses are most appropriate? (Choose two.)

options.text: Approve the PR, because a green CI run shows that the change preserves all of the expected behavior.
options.why: CI is green because the assertions were edited; the tests no longer independently check the original expected behavior.

options.text: Hold the PR until each changed assertion is justified against the spec.
options.why: Edited assertions can hide a regression; each change must be shown to reflect an intended behavior change.

options.text: Add a CLAUDE.md rule: don't edit existing assertions to make tests pass; flag the conflict.
options.why: A persistent project instruction prevents the pattern in future sessions and makes Claude surface the conflict instead.

options.text: Exclude test files from CI for Claude-authored PRs so that assertion edits no longer cause confusion.
options.why: Removing tests from CI eliminates the safety net rather than addressing the unreviewed assertion changes.

options.text: Ask the same Claude session whether its test changes were correct and approve the PR if it says yes.
options.why: The authoring session is biased toward its own work; independent verification against the spec is needed.

explanation: In code review of Claude-written changes, tests are the contract. Assertion edits in the same PR as a fix need explicit justification against the specification, and a CLAUDE.md rule helps prevent "make the tests pass" edits in future sessions. A green CI run built on rewritten assertions proves little.
reference: Claude Code docs — Best practices; Memory (CLAUDE.md)

stem: A team must migrate 1,800 Python 2 modules to Python 3 with Claude Code and wants the bulk of the work to run unattended overnight on a build machine. Which approach does Anthropic's guidance for large migrations recommend?

options.text: Open one interactive session, accept all edits automatically, and ask Claude to migrate every module in order.
options.why: A single session across 1,800 files exhausts context, is not unattended, and yields one enormous unreviewable change.

options.text: Start the per-file loop on all 1,800 modules at once with every permission check bypassed so the run never stalls.
options.why: Skipping the pilot means prompt flaws repeat 1,800 times, and bypassing permissions removes the guardrail for unattended runs.

options.text: Paste the modules into one very long prompt and ask Claude to return all of the converted code together.
options.why: One giant prompt cannot hold the codebase, gives Claude no tools to run tests, and produces unverifiable output.

options.text: Have Claude list the files, loop claude -p per file with scoped --allowedTools, and pilot on a few files first.
options.why: Fan-out with headless calls scales, scoped tools keep unattended runs safe, and piloting refines the prompt before the full run.

explanation: For large-scale refactors, Claude Code's guidance is to fan out: generate a task list, loop claude -p over it with --allowedTools restricting what Claude may do, refine the prompt on two or three files, and then run the full set, verifying results with tests. /batch offers a built-in variant using subagents in worktrees.
reference: Claude Code docs — Best practices (fan out across files)

stem: A nightly job syncs support tickets into a vector store for a Claude-powered assistant by paging through an internal REST API with ?offset=N&limit=100, sorted newest first. New tickets keep arriving during the sync, and each run has both duplicates and missing tickets. What is the best fix?

options.text: Switch to cursor (keyset) pagination on a stable sort key such as (created_at, id).
options.why: Keyset cursors are anchored to a record, not a position, so inserts during the sync cannot shift pages.

options.text: Reduce the page size to 10 so that fewer tickets move between pages while the job is running.
options.why: Smaller pages shrink each window but inserts still shift offsets, so duplicates and gaps continue.

options.text: Fetch all pages in parallel so the whole sync finishes before many new tickets can arrive.
options.why: Parallel offset reads narrow the timing window but remain position-based, so concurrent inserts still cause gaps.

options.text: Keep offset pagination but remove duplicates by ticket ID after the whole sync finishes.
options.why: Deduplication fixes the repeats but cannot recover the tickets that were skipped entirely.

explanation: Offset pagination over a changing, newest-first dataset is unstable: each insert shifts every later offset, producing both repeats and gaps. Cursor or keyset pagination on a unique, stable ordering (the same idea as has_more/after_id on Claude's list endpoints) gives a consistent traversal.
reference: Exam guide — Software Engineering Foundations (REST APIs)

stem: Claude's structured JSON output from an extraction service is consumed by three downstream services owned by other teams. The service must add a new field and rename customer_no to customer_id without breaking consumers that deploy on their own schedules. Which practices should the team follow? (Choose two.)

options.text: Rename the field in place and coordinate a same-day deploy of the extraction service and all three consumers.
options.why: Lockstep deploys across independent teams are fragile; any consumer that lags will break on the missing field.

options.text: Add customer_id and the new field while still populating customer_no until consumers migrate.
options.why: Additive changes keep old consumers working while new ones adopt the new fields, allowing the old one to be retired later.

options.text: Mark every field optional in the output schema so no future change can ever break validation.
options.why: Making everything optional disables useful validation and pushes missing-data failures downstream.

options.text: Version the schema, run contract tests for consumers in CI, and have consumers ignore unknown fields.
options.why: Versioning and contract tests catch breaking changes before release, and tolerant readers let new fields ship safely.

options.text: Let Claude pick field names at runtime from the document content so the schema adapts automatically.
options.why: Unstable field names make the output impossible for consumers to parse reliably.

explanation: JSON contracts between services evolve safely through additive, versioned changes: add new fields, keep deprecated ones populated during a migration window, test consumer contracts in CI, and design consumers as tolerant readers. The schema Claude fills should be as stable as any other API contract.
reference: Claude API docs — Structured outputs; Exam guide — Software Engineering Foundations

stem: In a monorepo, the root CLAUDE.md has grown with React conventions that matter only when Claude works on files under src/web/. Backend developers complain that the frontend rules crowd their sessions. How should the team restructure these instructions?

options.text: Move the React conventions into .claude/settings.json under a new frontend section.
options.why: settings.json holds configuration such as permissions and hooks, not instructions Claude reads as memory.

options.text: Move the React conventions into each frontend developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.
options.why: User-level files are personal and not version-controlled, so the team loses a shared, reviewed source.

options.text: Move them into a .claude/rules/ file whose paths frontmatter matches src/web/**.
options.why: Path-scoped rules load only when Claude works with matching files, keeping backend sessions lean.

options.text: Keep them in the root CLAUDE.md, but mark the section "frontend only" in bold.
options.why: The root file loads at every launch regardless of labels, so the context cost and noise remain.

explanation: Keep CLAUDE.md concise and move area-specific instructions into .claude/rules/ files with paths frontmatter. They load only when Claude reads matching files, which saves context and reduces conflicting guidance in unrelated work.
reference: Claude Code docs — Memory (organize rules with .claude/rules/)

stem: A repository's committed .claude/settings.json sets the team's default model to Sonnet. One developer wants Opus in this repository for their own sessions only, without changing anything for teammates. Where should they set it?

options.text: In ~/.claude/settings.json, since user settings take precedence over the project file.
options.why: User settings rank below shared project settings, so the team's value would still win in this repository.

options.text: In .claude/settings.local.json in the repository, which is kept out of git.
options.why: Project local settings rank above shared project settings and apply only to this developer in this project.

options.text: In the committed .claude/settings.json, changing the model and asking teammates to ignore it.
options.why: Editing the shared file changes the default for every teammate who pulls it.

options.text: In CLAUDE.md, adding a line that tells Claude to use the Opus model for this project.
options.why: CLAUDE.md is instruction context and does not select the model a session runs on.

explanation: Settings precedence from highest to lowest is managed, command line, project local (.claude/settings.local.json), shared project (.claude/settings.json), then user (~/.claude/settings.json). A personal override for one project belongs in the local file, which stays out of version control.
reference: Claude Code docs — Settings (settings precedence)

stem: Company policy says developers may use only Sonnet and Haiku in Claude Code. An admin committed an allowlist of those models to each repository's .claude/settings.json, but a developer added Opus to the list in their own user settings and could select it. Which approach enforces the policy?

options.text: Deploy the model allowlist (availableModels) in managed settings rather than project files.
options.why: Managed settings sit above every other scope, and a managed allowlist is applied as-is, ignoring additions in lower files.

options.text: Add a line to each repository's CLAUDE.md telling Claude to use only Sonnet or Haiku.
options.why: CLAUDE.md is context for Claude, not enforced configuration, and cannot restrict model selection.

options.text: Set the default model to Sonnet in every repository's settings so sessions always start on it.
options.why: A default only chooses the starting model; developers can still switch with /model.

options.text: Add a permissions deny rule for Opus to each repository so Claude Code refuses to use it.
options.why: Permission rules govern tool use such as Bash or Read, not which model a session may select.

explanation: Organization-wide policy belongs in managed settings, the only scope developers cannot override. List settings normally merge across user, project, and local files, which is why a developer could extend the project allowlist; a managed availableModels list is applied as-is.
reference: Claude Code docs — Settings (settings precedence; lists merge)

stem: A monorepo's root CLAUDE.md says "Use npm for all package commands." Later, packages/api/CLAUDE.md added "Use pnpm." When developers launch Claude Code from the repo root and work in packages/api, Claude sometimes runs npm and sometimes pnpm. What explains this, and what is the best fix?

options.text: The nested file fully overrides the root once loaded, so the root must be failing to load; run /init again to regenerate it.
options.why: CLAUDE.md files do not override each other, and regenerating the root file leaves the contradiction in place.

options.text: Claude reads only the root CLAUDE.md when launched from the root; move the pnpm rule into settings.json.
options.why: Subdirectory CLAUDE.md files load when Claude reads files there, and settings.json is not where instructions belong.

options.text: The files conflict because both load; prefix the pnpm rule with "IMPORTANT" so it takes priority.
options.why: Emphasis may shift which rule wins, but the files still contradict each other, so the behavior stays unreliable.

options.text: The files are combined, not overridden, so Claude may follow either; remove the contradiction.
options.why: Contradictory instructions can be resolved arbitrarily; making the root rule scoped or generic removes the conflict at its source.

explanation: Claude Code concatenates CLAUDE.md files (ancestors at launch, subdirectories on demand) rather than letting one override another. When two instructions contradict, Claude may pick either. Remove the conflict: keep root rules generic or explicitly scoped, and put package-specific instructions in that package's CLAUDE.md or a path-scoped rule.
reference: Claude Code docs — Memory (how CLAUDE.md files load)

stem: A team versions prompts in git and runs evals whenever a prompt changes. An engineer upgraded the pinned model ID in a separate config PR with no prompt change, so no evals ran, and extraction quality dropped because prompt v14 had been tuned for the old model. Which practices prevent a repeat? (Choose two.)

options.text: Version model ID, prompt, sampling parameters, and tool schemas together as one release unit.
options.why: Output quality depends on the combination, so versioning them as a unit makes every behavior-affecting change visible and reviewable.

options.text: Freeze the model ID permanently so that the tuned prompt never has to be re-validated.
options.why: Models are deprecated and retired, so a permanent freeze eventually forces an unplanned migration.

options.text: Run the eval gate in CI when any part of that configuration changes, not just the prompt.
options.why: The failure happened because a model-only change skipped the gate; gating on all elements closes that gap.

options.text: Run the eval suite on a weekly schedule instead of on each change to catch regressions in bulk.
options.why: A weekly run lets a regression reach production first and makes it harder to tie to the change that caused it.

options.text: Rename each prompt file to include the model name so engineers remember which model it targets.
options.why: A naming convention relies on memory and does not stop an untested pairing from shipping.

explanation: Prompt versioning and model pinning are two halves of one configuration problem: behavior comes from the model, prompt, parameters, and tools together. Version them as a release unit and run the eval gate whenever any part changes, then log that configuration version with each request.
reference: Claude API docs — Model IDs and versioning; Claude docs — Define success criteria and build evaluations

stem: A platform team maintains an internal Claude Code plugin marketplace. It wants backend engineers to install a standard set of five plugins with one command, and to be able to add a sixth plugin to that set later without every engineer changing their setup by hand. Which approach best fits?

options.text: Publish a README with five install commands and announce new additions in the team chat.
options.why: Manual steps drift across engineers and every later addition requires each person to act by hand.

options.text: Copy the five plugins' files into one large plugin so there is a single thing to install.
options.why: Merging forks every plugin, so the bundle stops receiving the original plugins' updates.

options.text: Ask each engineer to list the five plugins in their own ~/.claude/settings.json file.
options.why: Per-person configuration is not centrally versioned, and each addition still needs every engineer to edit a file.

options.text: Publish a bundle plugin listing the five as dependencies, and release a new version to add one.
options.why: Installing the bundle installs its dependencies, and a new bundle version adds the sixth plugin when engineers update.

explanation: Plugin dependencies are declared in the dependencies array of .claude-plugin/plugin.json. A plugin containing only a name and dependencies acts as a team bundle: one install brings in the whole set, and publishing a new bundle version (with a version range per dependency if needed) distributes changes centrally.
reference: Claude Code docs — Plugin dependencies (bundle plugins for a team)
